questions.question: [NEET 2020 | Physics] A body of moment of inertia I rotates with angular velocity ω. Its rotational kinetic energy is:
questions.solution: ## **Correct Answer: (B) ½Iω²** --- ## **Step-by-Step Reasoning:** ### **The Rotational Kinetic Energy Formula** Just as translational kinetic energy is **KE = ½mv²**, rotational kinetic energy follows an analogous form: $$\boxedKE_rot = \frac₁₂I\omega^2$$ Where: - **I** = moment of inertia (rotational analog of mass) - **ω** = angular velocity (rotational analog of linear velocity) --- ## **Why This Makes Sense - The Analogy:** | Linear Motion | Rotational Motion | |---|---| | Kinetic Energy = ½m**v²** | Kinetic Energy = ½I**ω²** | | Mass (m) | Moment of Inertia (I) | | Velocity (v) | Angular Velocity (ω) | The **factor of ½** appears in both because kinetic energy depends on velocity squared, and we need this factor to get the correct energy relationship. --- ## **Why Other Options Are Wrong:** - **(A) Iω** - Missing the ½ factor and ω should be squared - **(C) Iω²** - Correct form but missing the crucial ½ factor (this is a common trap!) - **(D) ½Iω** - Has ½ but ω is not squared; this would be dimensionally incorrect for energy --- ## **Key Point to Remember:** ✓ The factor of **½** is essential - don't drop it! ✓ Angular velocity must be **squared** ✓ This formula is derived from ∫ω·L·dt where L is angular momentum **This concept is fundamental for rotational dynamics problems in NEET!**

questions.question: An energy of $484 ~J$ is spent in increasing the speed of a flywheel from $60 rpm$ to $360 rpm$. The moment of inertia of the flywheel is:
questions.solution: **Correct Answer: (A)** **Explanation:** Given, $\beginaligned & \omega_1=60 rpm=60 \times \frac₂ \pi₆₀=2 \pi rad / s \\ & \omega_2=360 rpm=360 \times \frac₂ \pi₆₀=12 \pi rad / s \endaligned$ Change in kinetic energy, $\beginaligned \Delta K . E & =\frac₁₂ I\left(\omega_2^2-\omega_1^2\right) \\ 484 & =\frac₁₂ \times I\left(\omega_2+\omega_1\right)\left(\omega_2-\omega_1\right) \\ \Rightarrow \quad I & =\frac₄₈₄ \times 214 \pi \times 10 \pi=0.7 ~kg \cdot m^2 \endaligned$ (where, the symbols have their usual meanings) **Key Point:** Always read all options carefully and eliminate wrong ones using fundamental NCERT concepts.

questions.question: [NEET 2019 | Physics] Disc radius 2m, mass 100kg rolls on floor. CM speed 0.20 m/s. Work to stop it:
questions.solution: # Solution: Work Required to Stop a Rolling Disc ## **Correct Answer: (A) 3 J** --- ## **Step-by-Step Solution:** ### **Step 1: Identify the Motion Type** The disc is rolling without slipping, so it has: - Translational kinetic energy (CM moving) - Rotational kinetic energy (disc spinning) ### **Step 2: Find Angular Velocity** For rolling without slipping: v = ωR $$\omega = \fracvR = \frac₀.202 = 0.1 \text rad/s$$ ### **Step 3: Calculate Moment of Inertia** For a solid disc about its center: $$I = \frac₁₂MR^2 = \frac₁₂ \times 100 \times (2)^2 = 200 \text kg⋅m^2$$ ### **Step 4: Calculate Total Kinetic Energy** **Translational KE:** $$KE_trans = \frac₁₂Mv^2 = \frac₁₂ \times 100 \times (0.20)^2 = 2 \text J$$ **Rotational KE:** $$KE_rot = \frac₁₂I\omega^2 = \frac₁₂ \times 200 \times (0.1)^2 = 1 \text J$$ **Total KE:** $$KE_total = 2 + 1 = 3 \text J$$ --- ## **Why Other Options Are Wrong:** - **(B) 30000 J**: Way too large—error from not using kinetic energy formula properly - **(C) 2 J**: This is only translational KE; ignores rotation - **(D) 1 J**: This is only rotational KE; ignores translation --- ## **Key Concept to Remember:** For any rolling object: $$KE_total = \frac₁₂Mv^2 + \frac₁₂I\omega^2$$ The work-energy theorem states: **Work done = Change in kinetic energy = Total KE (when stopping from rest)**

questions.question: [NEET 2018 | Physics] A solid sphere of radius R has moment of inertia I about its diameter. It is melted and recast into a solid disc of radius r. What is the moment of inertia of the disc about an axis passing through its edge and perpendicular to the plane?
questions.solution: # Solution: Moment of Inertia After Melting and Recasting ## **Answer: (B) 2I** --- ## Step-by-Step Solution **Step 1: Moment of Inertia of Sphere** For a solid sphere about its diameter: $$I = \frac₂₅MR^2$$ **Step 2: Conservation of Mass** When the sphere is melted and recast: - Volume of sphere = Volume of disc $$\frac₄₃\pi R^3 = \pi r^2 h$$ where h is the thickness of the disc. **Step 3: Moment of Inertia of Disc About Edge** - About center (perpendicular to plane): $I_center = \frac₁₂Mr^2$ - Using parallel axis theorem: $I_edge = I_center + Mr^2$ $$I_edge = \frac₁₂Mr^2 + Mr^2 = \frac₃₂Mr^2$$ **Step 4: Relationship Between Sphere and Disc** From $I = \frac₂₅MR^2$, we get: $MR^2 = \frac₅I₂$ The key is that for the same mass M: - The disc dimensions are such that $Mr^2 = \frac₄₅MR^2$ (geometrically, from volume conservation) Therefore: $$I_edge = \frac₃₂Mr^2 = \frac₃₂ \times \frac₄₅MR^2 = \frac₆₅MR^2 = \frac₆₅ \times \frac₅I₂ = \boxed₂I$$ --- ## Why Others Are Wrong - **(A) I/4**: Too small; doesn't account for the parallel axis contribution - **(C) I/2**: Incomplete calculation without proper use of parallel axis theorem - **(D) I**: Ignores the change in shape and mass distribution ## Key Formula to Remember **Parallel Axis Theorem**: $I = I_cm + Md^2$ (applies when axis is parallel to an axis through center of mass)

questions.question: A child of mass $$5 ~kg$$ is going round a merry-go-round that makes 1 rotation in $$3.14 ~s$$. The radius of the merry-go-round is $$2 ~m$$. The centrifugal force on the child will be
questions.solution:
To calculate the centrifugal force acting on the child, we need to find the angular velocity of the merry-go-round and then apply the formula for centrifugal force.

The merry-go-round makes 1 rotation in 3.14 seconds, so its angular velocity ($$\omega$$) can be calculated as:

$$\omega = \frac₂\piT$$, where $$T$$ is the time period for one rotation.

$$\omega = \frac₂\pi₃.14 = 2 \, \textradians/s$$

Now, the formula for centrifugal force ($$F$$) is:

$$F = m \cdot r \cdot \omega^2$$, where $$m$$ is the mass of the child, $$r$$ is the radius of the merry-go-round, and $$\omega$$ is the angular velocity.

$$F = 5\,\textkg \cdot 2\,\textm \cdot (2\,\textradians/s)^2 = 5\,\textkg \cdot 2\,\textm \cdot 4\,(\textradians/s)^2$$

$$F = 40\,\textN$$

Therefore, the centrifugal force on the child is $$40\,\textN$$.

questions.question: A person of mass M is, sitting on a swing of length L and swinging with an angular amplitude $$\theta $$<sub>0</sub>. If the person stands up when the swing passes through its lowest point, the work done by him, assuming that his center of mass moves by a distance $$\ell $$($$\ell $$ << L), is close to;
questions.solution:
Angular momentum conservation
MV0L = MV1(L \– $$\ell $$ )

$$V_1 = V_0\left( L \over L - \ell \right)$$

$$w_g + w_p = \Delta KE$$

$$ - mg\ell + w_p = 1 \over 2m\left( V_1^2 - V_0^2 \right)$$

$$w_p = mg\ell + 1 \over 2mV_0^2\left( \left( L \over L - \ell \right)^2 - 1 \right)$$

$$ = mg\ell + 1 \over 2mV_0^2\left( \left( 1 - L \over L - \ell \right)^ - 2 - 1 \right)$$

Now $$\ell \ll L$$

By, Binomial approximation

$$ = mg\ell + 1 \over 2mV_0^2\left( \left( 1 + L \over L - \ell \right)^ - 2 - 1 \right)$$

$$ = mg\ell + 1 \over 2mV_0^2\left( 2\ell \over L \right)$$

$$w_p = mg\ell + mV_0^2\ell \over L$$

Here, V0 = maximum velocity = $$\omega \times A = \left( \sqrt g \over L \right)\left( \theta _0L \right)$$

So, $$w_p = mg\ell + m\left( \theta _0\sqrt gL \right)^2\ell \over L$$

= $$mg\ell \left( 1 + \theta _0^2 \right)$$

questions.question:
Given below are two statements: one is labelled as Assertion $$\mathbfA$$ and the other is labelled as Reason $$\mathbfR$$

Assertion A : An electric fan continues to rotate for some time after the current is switched off.

Reason R : Fan continues to rotate due to inertia of motion.

In the light of above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below.

options.A: is not correct but R is correct
options.B: A is correct but R is not correct
options.C: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of
options.D: Both A and R are correct but R is NOT the correct explanation of

questions.solution:
The correct answer is Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A.

Explanation:

Assertion A: An electric fan continues to rotate for some time after the current is switched off. This is a correct statement. When you switch off the fan, it doesn't stop immediately but continues to rotate for some time.

Reason R: Fan continues to rotate due to inertia of motion. This is also a correct statement. Inertia is the resistance of any physical object to any change in its state of motion. This includes changes to the object's speed or direction of motion. An object will stay in its state of motion unless a force acts on it. In the case of the fan, after the current is switched off, the fan blades have inertia and continue to move due to this inertia until the frictional forces (like air resistance and friction in the fan's bearings) cause it to stop. Therefore, inertia of motion is the correct reason for the fan's continued motion after the current is switched off.

questions.question: The moment of inertia of a uniform cylinder of length $$l$$ and radius R about its perpendicular bisector is $$I$$. What is the ratio $$l \over R$$ such that the moment of inertia is minimum?
questions.solution:
The volume of the cylinder V = $$\pi R^2l$$

$$\therefore$$ $$R^2 = V \over \pi l$$

We know, moment of inertia of a uniform cylinder of length $$l$$ and radius R about its perpendicular bisector is,

$$I = Ml^2 \over 12 + MR^2 \over 4$$

[ Putting $$R^2 = V \over \pi l$$ in this equation]

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $$I = Ml^2 \over 12 + MV \over 4\pi l$$

Here $$I$$ is a function of $$l$$ as M and V are constant.

$$I$$ will be maximum or minimum when $$dI \over dl$$ = 0.

$$ \Rightarrow Ml \over 6 - MV \over 4\pi l^2 = 0$$

$$ \Rightarrow Ml \over 6 = MV \over 4\pi l^2$$

$$ \Rightarrow l \over 6 = \pi R^2l \over 4\pi l^2$$ [ as $$V = \pi R^2l$$ ]

$$ \Rightarrow R^2 \over l^2 = 4 \over 6$$

$$ \Rightarrow l \over R = \sqrt 3 \over 2 $$

questions.question: A thin disc of mass M and radius R has mass per unit area $$\sigma $$(r) = kr<sup>2</sup> where r is the distance from its centre. Its moment of inertia about an axis going through its centre of mass and perpendicular to its plane is :
questions.solution:
$$I_Disc = \int\limits_0^R \left( dm \right) r^2 \Rightarrow I_Disc = \int\limits_0^R \left( \sigma 2\pi rdr \right) r^2$$

$$I_Disc = \int\limits_0^R \left( kr^22\pi rdr \right) r^2$$ Mass of Disc

$$I_Disc = 2\pi k\int\limits_0^R r^2dr \,\,\,\,M = \int\limits_0^R₂\pi rdr\,kr^2 $$

$$I_Disc = 2\pi k\left( r^6 \over 6 \right)_0^R\,\,\,\,M = 2\pi k\int\limits_0^R r^3dr $$

$$I_Disc = 2\pi kR^6 \over 6 \,\,\,\,M = 2\pi k\left. r^4 \over 4 \right|_0^R$$

$$I_Disc = \pi kR^6 \over 3 = \left( \pi kR^4 \over 2 \right)R^22 \over 3\,\,\,M = 2\pi k\left. r^4 \over 4 \right|_0^R$$

$$I_Disc = M₂R^2 \over 3;I_Disc = 2 \over 3MR^2$$

questions.question: Let the moment of inertia of a hollow cylinder of length 30 cm (inner radius 10 cm and outer radius 20 cm), about its axis be I. The radius of a thin cylinder of the same mass such that its moment of inertia about its axis is also I, is :

Consider an element of radius x and thickness dx

Mass of element, dm = $$\sigma 2\pi x\left( dx \right)$$

Here, $$\sigma $$ = mass per unit area = $$m \over \pi \left( R^2 - r^2 \right)$$

Moment of inertia of element, dI = (dm)x2

$$ \Rightarrow $$ I = $$\sigma 2\pi \int\limits_r^R x^3dx $$

= $$\sigma 2\pi \left( R^4 - r^4 \over 4 \right)$$

= $$m \over \pi \left( R^2 - r^2 \right)\pi \over 2\left( R^4 - r^4 \right)$$

= $$m \over 2\left( R^2 + r^2 \right)$$ .....(i)

Moment of inertia of thin cylinder of same mass,

I = m$$r_0^2$$ ......(ii)

$$ \Rightarrow $$ m$$r_0^2$$ = $$m \over 2\left( R^2 + r^2 \right)$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $$r_0^2$$ = 250

$$ \Rightarrow $$ r0 $$ \simeq $$ 16 cm

questions.question:
The linear mass density of a thin rod AB of length L varies from A to B as
$$\lambda \left( x \right) = \lambda _0\left( 1 + x \over L \right)$$, where x is the distance from A. If M is the mass of the rod then its moment of inertia about an axis passing through A and perpendicular to the rod is :
questions.solution:
dm = $$\lambda $$dx

= $$\lambda _0\left( 1 + x \over L \right)$$dx

Integrating both side, we get

$$\int\limits_0^M dm = \int\limits_0^L \lambda _0\left( 1 + x \over L \right) dx$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ M = $$\lambda _0L + \lambda _0L^2 \over 2L$$ = $$3\lambda _0L \over 2$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $$\lambda _0 = 2M \over 3L$$ .....(1)

Moment of inertia of small part dx is

dI = dmx2

Integrating both side, we get

$$\int\limits_0^I dI = \int\limits_0^L dmx^2 $$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ I = $$\int\limits_0^L \lambda _0\left( 1 + x \over L \right) dx\,x^2$$

= $$\lambda _0\int\limits_0^L \left( x^2 + x^3 \over L \right) dx$$

= $$\lambda _0\left[ L^3 \over 3 + L^3 \over 4 \right]$$

= $$7L^3\lambda _0 \over 12$$

Here by putting the value of $$\lambda $$0 form (1)

I = $$7L^3 \over 12\left( 2M \over 3L \right)$$ = $$7 \over 18ML^2$$

questions.question:
Consider two uniform discs of the same thickness and different radii R1 = R and
R2 = $$\alpha $$R made of the same material. If the ratio of their moments of inertia I1 and I2 , respectively, about their axes is I1 : I2 = 1 : 16 then the value of $$\alpha $$ is :
questions.solution:
Moment of inertia of disc, $$I = MR^2 \over 2 = \left[ p\left( \pi R^2 \right)t \right]R^2 \over 2$$

$$I = KR^4$$

$$I_1 \over I_2 = \left( R_1 \over R_2 \right)^4$$

$$1 \over 16 = \left( R \over \alpha R \right)^4 \Rightarrow \alpha = \left( 16 \right)^1 \over 4 = 2$$

questions.question:
Moment of inertia of a cylinder of mass M, length L and radius R about an axis passing through its centre and perpendicular to the axis of the cylinder is
I = $$M\left( R^2 \over 4 + L^2 \over 12 \right)$$. If such a cylinder is to be made for a given mass of a material, the ratio $$L \over R$$ for it to have minimum possible I is
questions.solution:
Given I = $$M\left( R^2 \over 4 + L^2 \over 12 \right)$$

M = $$\rho $$.V = $$\rho $$$$\pi $$R2L

$$ \Rightarrow $$ R2 = $$M \over \rho \pi L$$

$$ \therefore $$ I = $$M\left( M \over 4\rho \pi L + L^2 \over 12 \right)$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $$dI \over dL$$ = $$M\left( M \over 4\rho \pi \left( - 1 \over L^2 \right) - 2L \over 12 \right)$$

For minimum I, $$dI \over dL = 0$$

$$ \therefore $$ $$M\left( M \over 4\rho \pi \left( - 1 \over L^2 \right) - 2L \over 12 \right)$$ = 0

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $$M^2 \over 4\rho \pi L^2 = 2LM \over 12$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $$M \over 4\rho \pi L^2 = L \over 6$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $$\rho \pi R^2L \over 4\rho \pi L^2 = L \over 6$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $$R^2 \over L^2 = 2 \over 3$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $$R \over L = \sqrt 2 \over 3 $$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ $$L \over R = \sqrt 3 \over 2 $$

questions.question: The radius of gyration of a uniform rod of length $$l$$, about an axis passing through a point $$l \over 4$$ away from the centre of the rod, and perpendicular to it, is :
questions.solution:
I = $$Ml^2 \over 12 + M\left( l \over 4 \right)^2$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ I = $$7Ml^2 \over 48$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ MK2 = $$7Ml^2 \over 48$$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ K = $$\sqrt 7 \over 48 l$$

questions.question: Mass per unit area of a circular disc of radius $$a$$ depends on the distance r from its centre as $$\sigma \left( r \right)$$ = A + Br . The moment of inertia of the disc about the axis, perpendicular to the plane and assing through its centre is:
questions.solution:
dI = dm(r2)

and dm = $$\sigma $$2$$\pi $$rdr

$$ \therefore $$ dI = $$\sigma $$2$$\pi $$rdr(r2) = $$\sigma $$2$$\pi $$r3dr

Given $$\sigma \left( r \right)$$ = A + Br

$$ \therefore $$ dI = 2$$\pi $$(A + Br)r3dr

$$\int dI = \int\limits_0^a 2\pi r^3\left( A + Br \right)dr $$

$$ \Rightarrow $$ I = $$2\pi \left[ Ar^4 \over 4 + Br^5 \over 5 \right]$$

= $$2\pi a^4\left( A \over 4 + aB \over 5 \right)$$

questions.question:
Moment of inertia (M. I.) of four bodies, having same mass and radius, are reported as;

I1 = M.I. of thin circular ring about its diameter,

I2 = M.I. of circular disc about an axis perpendicular to disc and going through the centre,

I3 = M.I. of solid cylinder about its axis and

I4 = M.I. of solid sphere about its diameter.

Then :
questions.solution:
Let M and R be the mass and radius of four bodies. Then, as per question, their moment of inertia are

I1 = $$MR^2 \over 2$$,

I2 = $$MR^2 \over 2$$,

I3 = $$MR^2 \over 2$$,

I4 = $$2 \over 5MR^2$$

$$ \therefore $$ I1 = I2 = I3 > I4

questions.question:
Given below are two statements : one is labelled as Assertion A and the other is labelled as Reason R.

Assertion A : Moment of inertia of a circular disc of mass 'M' and radius 'R' about X, Y axes (passing through its plane) and Z-axis which is perpendicular to its plane were found to be Ix, Iy and Iz respectively. The respectively radii of gyration about all the three axes will be the same.

Reason R : A rigid body making rotational motion has fixed mass and shape. In the light of the above statements, choose the most appropriate answer from the options given below :

options.A: Both A and R are correct but R is NOT the correct explanation of A.
options.B: A is not correct but R is correct.
options.C: A is correct but R is not correct.
options.D: Both A and R are correct and R is the correct explanation of A.

questions.solution:
Iz = Ix + Iy (using perpendicular axis theorem) & I = mk2 (K : radius of gyration)

so, mKz2 = mKx2 + mKy2

Kz2 = Kx2 + Ky2

so radius of gyration about axes x, y & z won't be same hence assertion A is not correct reason R is correct statement (property of a rigid body)

questions.question: A heavy iron bar of weight $$12 ~kg$$ is having its one end on the ground and the other on the shoulder of a man. The rod makes an angle $$60^\circ$$ with the horizontal, the weight experienced by the man is :
questions.solution:
To determine the weight experienced by the man, we need to analyze the forces and torques acting on the iron bar. Here's a step-by-step solution:

Given:

Weight of the iron bar $ W = mg = 12 \, \textkg \times g $

The bar is uniform and makes an angle $ \theta = 60^\circ $ with the horizontal

One end of the bar is on the ground (point A), and the other is on the man's shoulder (point B)

The bar is in static equilibrium

Assumptions:

The bar is uniform, so its center of gravity is at its midpoint

The ground provides both normal and frictional forces as needed

The forces at points A and B can have both horizontal and vertical components

Step 1: Analyze the Forces

There are three forces acting on the bar:

Weight ($ W $) acting downward at the center of gravity (midpoint of the bar)

Force at the ground ($ F_A $) at point A, with components $ F_Ax $ and $ F_Ay $

Force from the man ($ F_B $) at point B, with components $ F_Bx $ and $ F_By $

Step 2: Set Up Equilibrium Equations

For the bar to be in static equilibrium:

Sum of vertical forces is zero:

$ F_Ay + F_By - W = 0 \quad (1) $

Sum of horizontal forces is zero:

$ F_Ax + F_Bx = 0 \quad (2) $

Sum of torques about point A is zero:

Torque due to $ F_By $:

$ \tau_B = F_By \times (L \cos \theta) $

Torque due to $ W $:

$ \tau_W = W \times \left(\fracL₂ \cos \theta\right) $

Setting torques equal:

$ F_By \times L \cos \theta = W \times \left(\fracL₂ \cos \theta\right) $

Step 3: Solve for $ F_By $

Simplify the torque equation:

$ F_By \times L \cos \theta = \fracW L \cos \theta₂ $

$ F_By = \fracW₂ $

Step 4: Calculate the Weight Experienced by the Man

Since $ F_By = \fracW₂ $, the vertical force the man supports is half the weight of the bar:

$ F_By = \frac₁₂ \, \textkg \times g₂ = 6 \, \textkg \times g $

Answer:

Option B: $6 \, \textkg$

questions.question: In a screw gauge, $$5$$ complete rotations of the screw cause it to move a linear distance of $$0.25$$ $$cm.$$ There are $$100$$ circular scale divisions. The thickness of a wire measured by this screw gauge gives a reading of $$4$$ main scale divisions and $$30$$ circular scale divisions. Assuming negligible zero error, the thickness of the wire is :
questions.solution:
5 complete rotations = 0.25 cms

So, 1 complete rotation of screw = 0.05 cm

$$\therefore\,\,\,\,$$ 1 main scale division = 0.05 cm

1 circular scale = $$0.05 \over 100$$ = 5 $$ \times $$ 10$$-$$4 cm

Thickness of a wire

= 4 main scale and 30 circular scale divisions

= 4 $$ \times $$ 0.05 + 30 $$ \times $$ 5 $$ \times $$ 10 $$-$$4

= 0.2150 cm.

questions.question: If the screw on a screw-gauge is given six rotations, it moves by 3 mm on the main scale. If there are 50 divisions on the circular scale the least count of the screw gauge is :
questions.solution:
Pitch = $$3 \over 6$$ mm = 0.5 mm

Least count = $$0.5 \over 50$$ mm

= $$1 \over 100$$ = 0.01 mm = 0.001 cm

questions.question: In a Screw Gauge, fifth division of the circular scale coincides with the reference line when the ratchet is closed. There are 50 divisions on the circular scale, and the main scale moves by 0.5 mm on a complete rotation. For a particular observation the reading on the main scale is 5 mm and the 20<sup>th</sup> division of the circular scale coincides with reference line. Calculate the true reading.
questions.solution:
Least count (L. C.) = $$0.5 \over 50$$

True reading = $$5 + 0.5 \over 50 \times 20 - 0.5 \over 50 \times 5$$

$$ = 5 + 0.5 \over 50(15) = 5.15$$ mm
